**My recommendation: don't run production on 3.13t.** It's still experimental, and wheel makers are now dropping it. If you want no-GIL, the realistic path is 3.14t. That needs an exception to your platform's 3.13 pin.

**Findings (primary sources)**

1. **3.13t is officially experimental.** The CPython 3.13 docs say to "expect some bugs and a substantial single-threaded performance hit." Single-threaded code runs about 40% slower on pyperformance because the specializing interpreter is turned off. Other known problems: some objects are made immortal and never freed, so memory can grow; sharing an iterator or touching a frame across threads can crash; and importing a C extension that isn't marked free-thread-safe silently turns the GIL back on, with only a warning. https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html
2. **3.14t is the supported version.** PEP 779 (Final, accepted June 2025) puts 3.13 in Phase I (experimental) and 3.14 in Phase II (supported but optional). Its target is no more than 15% single-thread slowdown and about 20% more memory. https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ The 3.14 What's New confirms official support and puts the single-thread penalty at about 5–10%. https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.14.html
3. **Builders are dropping 3.13t.**
   - According to a PyTorch post, pypa/manylinux removed cp313t from its images on 2026-05-07, and PyTorch dropped 3.13t as a result. https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386
   - Pillow 12.3.0 removed its 3.13t wheels. https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/latest/releasenotes/12.3.0.html
   - cibuildwheel 3.4.1 deprecated cp313t builds. https://newreleases.io/project/github/pypa/cibuildwheel/release/v3.4.1
4. **Your three dependencies:**
   - **lxml is the blocker.** Its changelog says free-threading support is "enabled in Python 3.14t and later," and only in 7.0.0a1 (still at rc1, no final release). Current 6.1.3 on PyPI has cp314t wheels but none for cp313t. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lxml/lxml/master/CHANGES.txt, https://pypi.org/project/lxml/
   - **NumPy** added 3.13t support in 2.1.0. The latest release, 2.5.4, has cp314t manylinux wheels, and I found no cp313t wheel in its listing. The 2.5.0 notes report better ufunc scaling under free-threading. https://pypi.org/project/numpy/, https://numpy.org/devdocs/release/2.5.0-notes.html
   - **pydantic-core** added 3.13t support in 2.29.0. Latest 2.50.4 (Nov 2026) has cp314t wheels, and I found no cp313t wheels. https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/
   - The community tracker lists the first free-threaded versions as NumPy 2.1.0, pydantic 2.11 / pydantic-core 2.29, and lxml 7.0.0. https://py-free-threading.github.io/tracking/

**What I'd suggest**
- Ask for a 3.14t exception, or stay on GIL 3.13 and use multiprocessing for CPU-bound work.
- On 3.14t, check `sys._is_gil_enabled()` at startup. With lxml 6.x the GIL probably comes back on (I haven't confirmed this).
- Load-test with `PYTHON_GIL=0` and treat it as a pilot, not general rollout.

**What I'm unsure of**
- PyPI file listings were cut off when I fetched them. I didn't see cp313t wheels for NumPy, pydantic-core or lxml in the parts I read, but I can't rule out that some exist in the unseen parts.
- The manylinux removal date comes from the PyTorch post. I didn't read the manylinux changelog itself.
- I didn't check whether the cp314t lxml 6.1.3 wheel declares itself free-thread-safe or re-enables the GIL on import.
- I didn't look for pydantic thread-safety caveats or measure performance for your workload.

**Report to coordinator: press, forums, issue trackers and community write-ups**

**Short answer: no. 3.13t is a dead end, and the ecosystem is dropping it.** Free-threading is only officially supported starting with 3.14t. For this stack, the realistic goal is 3.14t, and only after lxml 7.0 is released.

**Findings**

1. **The 3.13 docs call the free-threaded build "experimental"** and warn of "some bugs and a substantial single-threaded performance hit" of about 40%. Two reasons: the specializing interpreter is turned off, and some objects are kept in memory forever, which can grow memory use. Sharing iterators or frame objects between threads can crash the program. https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html
2. **PEP 779 (accepted June 2025) makes free-threading "supported" from 3.14 onward**, with a cap of 15% single-thread slowdown. https://peps.python.org/pep-779/ · https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-779-criteria-for-supported-status-for-free-threaded-python/84319
3. **The standard Linux wheel-build images (manylinux) removed 3.13t on 2026-05-07, so most packages can no longer easily ship 3.13t builds.** As a result, PyTorch dropped 3.13t and tells users to move to 3.14t. https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386 Earlier, cibuildwheel began warning that cp313t was deprecated (PR #2787, April 2026), and Pillow 12.3 removed its 3.13t wheels. https://hugovk-pillow.readthedocs.io/en/latest/_sources/releasenotes/12.3.0.rst.txt
4. **NumPy 2.5.4 (Oct 2026) has no cp313t wheels in its file list.** It has cp314t for manylinux x86-64. https://pypi.org/project/numpy/
5. **pydantic-core added 3.13t support in 2.29.0, and 2.34.1 still had cp313t wheels.** The current 2.50.4 (Nov 2026) ships only cp314t and cp315t free-threaded wheels. https://newreleases.io/project/pypi/pydantic-core/release/2.29.0 · https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/
6. **lxml is the main blocker.**
   - Its bug tracker reports that the test suite crashed on 3.13.3t.
   - The cp314t wheels starting with 6.0.2 quietly turn the GIL back on when imported. Using lxml from several threads with the GIL forced off was expected to crash.
   - The fix is targeted at lxml 7.0. Only 7.0.0a1 (an alpha, May 2026) is out so far, and it targets 3.14t and later.
   - Latest stable is 6.1.3 (Sep 2026). I found no cp313t wheels for it.
   https://bugs.launchpad.net/lxml/+bug/2111289 · https://pypi.org/project/lxml/
7. **Silent GIL re-enable is a known trap.** If any extension isn't marked thread-safe, the GIL turns back on and the speedup disappears without an obvious error. https://pycon.de/archive/2026/talks/are-we-free-threaded-ready-looking-at-where-free-threaded-python-fails/
8. **3.14t still has open CPython crash reports, mostly in garbage collection and shutdown paths.** https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/141965 · https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/142421
9. **Community tracker:** https://py-free-threading.github.io/tracking lists lxml as 7.0.0.

**What to do:** Drop the 3.13t plan. To get free-threading, get the platform's 3.13 pin lifted to 3.14. Add a separate 3.14t CI job, check `sys._is_gil_enabled()` at startup, and audit your own shared mutable state. Wait for lxml 7.0 final; until then, put a lock around lxml calls. Measure single-thread overhead against the GIL build. Until then, use multiprocessing on 3.13 instead.

**What I'm unsure of**
- I only read part of the lxml and pydantic-core PyPI pages, so older cp313t wheels may exist that I didn't see.
- I don't know whether lxml 7.0 final has shipped.
- I found no detailed first-hand production account for 3.13t or 3.14t. Community overhead figures (for example, "5–10% on 3.14t") are unverified.
- I couldn't open Quansight's one-year recap (HTTP 429).

## Report: independent measurements, critiques, counter-evidence

**Bottom line:** No. 3.13t isn't production-ready for this service, and the ecosystem has largely moved past it. If free-threading is the goal, unpin to 3.14t and benchmark your own workload there.

**Findings**

1. **The CPython docs call 3.13t experimental.** They say to expect bugs and about a **40% single-thread slowdown on pyperformance**, mainly because the specializing interpreter is turned off. Known hazards: sharing an iterator between threads can crash or skip items, touching frames from other threads can crash, and a lot of objects become immortal, which raises memory use. https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html
2. **3.14 is the officially supported phase (PEP 779).** The targets are ≤15% single-thread overhead (about 10% measured) and ≤20% extra memory (about 15–20% measured). https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ The current docs give an average overhead of 1–8%, with x86-64 Linux at the high end. https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html
3. **The ecosystem is dropping 3.13t.** manylinux took 3.13t out of its images on 7 May 2026, and PyTorch dropped cp313t and tells users to move to 3.14t. https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386 cibuildwheel has also deprecated cp313t. https://discuss.python.org/t/how-to-make-cibuildwheel-support-for-cp313t-and-cp314t/105429
4. **None of your three dependencies' latest releases showed a cp313t wheel in the parts of PyPI I could read. All three ship cp314t.**
   - lxml 6.1.3: cp314t and cp315t only. https://pypi.org/project/lxml/6.1.3/#files
   - pydantic-core 2.50.4: cp314t and cp315t. https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/#files Free-threaded 3.13t support first came in 2.29.0. https://newreleases.io/project/pypi/pydantic-core/release/2.29.0
   - NumPy 2.5.4: cp314t. https://pypi.org/project/numpy/#files
   
   On 3.13t you'd be stuck on older pinned versions or building from source.
5. **NumPy's free-threading support is still labelled experimental.** Sharing arrays between threads is only safe read-only. Object arrays can have data races, and resizing an array while another thread uses it can crash the interpreter. https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/thread_safety.html
6. **Independent benchmarks show it can get slower.** On 3.14.0b2, a threaded nearest-neighbour benchmark took **3.61 s with the GIL off vs 2.38 s with it on**. Core devs traced this to reference-count contention on shared objects, and the fix was to give each thread its own data. https://discuss.python.org/t/slower-performance-with-disable-gil-on-threaded-nearest-neighbor-benchmark-10m-points/95365 CodSpeed found threads beat processes on 3.13t, but said the single-thread overhead makes it not production-ready. https://codspeed.io/blog/state-of-python-3-13-performance-free-threading Informal 3.13t overhead figures run from about 17% to 40%. https://buttondown.com/ckae930413/archive/python-gil-vs-free-threading-313t-cpu-benchmark/ A pure-Python web server on 3.13t went only from 1.9× at 8 threads to 2.1× at 16, and the author calls it "not production-ready". https://discuss.python.org/t/experimenting-with-free-threaded-python-3-13-for-web-frameworks/106318

**Recommendation:** Don't ship on 3.13t. Make a case to move the platform pin to 3.14t. Then:
- Check that `sys._is_gil_enabled()` returns False after importing lxml. If an extension doesn't declare free-threading support, the GIL gets re-enabled without an error.
- Benchmark your real request mix at 1 thread and at N threads against GIL 3.14 and against multiprocessing.
- Avoid mutating shared objects (arrays, models, iterators) in hot paths.

**What I'm unsure of**
- The PyPI file listings were cut off, so I can't fully rule out cp313t wheels in the latest releases. Older releases definitely had some, e.g. pydantic-core ≥2.29 and NumPy ≥2.1.
- I couldn't confirm whether lxml marks itself as safe to run without the GIL; its changelog doesn't mention free-threading.
- I found no pydantic-specific measurements of how validation scales across threads.
- The informal overhead numbers come from blogs and vary a lot.

# Is free-threaded 3.13t production-ready for your service?

**No.** The best path to no-GIL is 3.14t, which means asking for an exception to your 3.13 pin. Even on 3.14t, lxml will probably turn the GIL back on until lxml 7.0 is final.

## Why not 3.13t

- **It is officially experimental.** The CPython docs warn of bugs and about a 40% single-thread slowdown. They also list memory growth from immortal objects and crashes when iterators or frames are shared across threads. https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html
- **3.14 is the first supported phase.** PEP 779 sets that status, with a target of at most 15% single-thread overhead. https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ Official 3.14 figures put the overhead at roughly 1–10%. https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.14.html
- **The ecosystem is dropping 3.13t.**
  - manylinux removed cp313t on 2026-05-07, and PyTorch followed. https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386
  - Pillow 12.3 dropped its cp313t wheels. https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/latest/releasenotes/12.3.0.html
- **Your dependencies' current releases show cp314t wheels but no cp313t ones.** The researchers saw only partial PyPI file lists, so this isn't certain. On 3.13t you would be stuck on older pins, such as pydantic-core 2.34.1, or building from source.
  - https://pypi.org/project/numpy/
  - https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/
  - https://pypi.org/project/lxml/

## The lxml blocker

Per lxml's bug tracker, its cp314t wheels re-enable the GIL on import. Forcing the GIL off was expected to crash. The fix is targeted at lxml 7.0, and only an alpha had been found. https://bugs.launchpad.net/lxml/+bug/2111289

## Other caveats

- NumPy's free-threading support is still labelled experimental, and arrays are only safe to share read-only. https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/thread_safety.html
- Turning the GIL off can make code slower. One threaded benchmark took 3.61 s without the GIL versus 2.38 s with it, because of refcount contention on shared objects. https://discuss.python.org/t/slower-performance-with-disable-gil-on-threaded-nearest-neighbor-benchmark-10m-points/95365
- 3.14t still has open crash reports. https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/141965

## What to do

1. **Now:** stay on GIL 3.13 and use multiprocessing for CPU-bound work.
2. **Request a 3.14t exception** and add a separate 3.14t CI job.
3. **Check the GIL at startup.** Assert `sys._is_gil_enabled()` is `False` after all imports, because the GIL can come back silently.
4. **Wait for lxml 7.0 final**, or put a lock around lxml calls when running with `PYTHON_GIL=0`.
5. **Benchmark your real workload** at 1 thread and at N threads, against both GIL 3.14 and multiprocessing. Avoid mutating shared arrays, models or iterators in hot paths.
6. **Pilot before rolling out** generally.

**Open question:** whether lxml 7.0 final has shipped. Check its changelog before planning: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lxml/lxml/master/CHANGES.txt

**Primary sources: report to coordinator**

**Findings**

1. **Origin of the 91% figure.** It comes from AHA EPI|Lifestyle 2024 Abstract P192 (Zhong lab, Shanghai Jiao Tong), which used NHANES 2003–2018 data on about 20,000 adults. Eating duration came from **two 24-hour dietary recalls** at baseline, and deaths were followed for a median of 8 years. People eating in under 8 hours were compared with a 12–16 h reference group. The AHA itself said abstracts are "preliminary," not peer-reviewed. The senior author said the result does not show that time-restricted eating (TRE) *causes* cardiovascular death, and Christopher Gardner noted that diet quality was not accounted for. https://newsroom.heart.org/news/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-linked-to-a-91-higher-risk-of-cardiovascular-death

2. **Peer-reviewed version.** Chen…Zhong, *Diabetes Metab Syndr* 2025;19(7):103278, PMID 40849219. It has n=19,831 and a 12–14 h reference group. For under 8 h: **HR 2.35 (95% CI 1.39–3.98)** for CVD death. There was **no association with all-cause or cancer mortality**, and the authors say residual confounding may explain the result. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:40849219&resultType=core&format=json ; https://medicaldialogues.in/amp/diet-nutrition/news/intermittent-fasting-under-8-hours-may-raise-heart-death-risk-by-135-percent-study-finds-153915

3. **Independent NHANES analysis.** Mao et al., *Aging Cell* 2025 (n=33,052, 1,277 CVD deaths) found a U-shaped curve, with the lowest mortality at about 11–12 h/day. Windows of 8 h or less were linked to about 30% higher all-cause and over 50% higher CVD mortality, mainly in older adults. It uses the same dataset and the same 2-day recall method. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40944446/

4. **Expert criticism.** UK experts (McConway, Spiegelhalter, Frayn, Sanders, Mellor, Leurent) pointed out:
   - Two days of recall don't capture habitual eating, and a short recorded window may just mean an incomplete record.
   - Reverse causation: people already at risk may restrict their eating.
   - Shift work, poverty and stress could explain both the eating pattern and the risk.
   - Body weight, lipids and blood pressure were unknown.

   https://www.sciencemediacentre.org/expert-reaction-to-conference-abstract-about-time-restricted-eating-and-cardiovascular-death/

   Varady and more than 30 researchers disputed the study. They noted the <8 h group had 60% more smokers and 250% more Black participants than the reference group. https://www.nutritioninsight.com/news/scientists-dispute-study-linking-time-restricted-eating-to-poor-heart-health.html

   McGill OSS counted 1 positive result among about 36 analyses and suggested it may be chance. https://www.mcgill.ca/oss/article/medical-health-and-nutrition/intermittent-fasting-and-perils-fast-facts

5. **Randomized trial evidence (intermediate outcomes only, no trials on mortality).**
   - BMJ 2025 network meta-analysis (99 RCTs, n=6,582, mostly about 12 weeks long): TRE gives weight loss similar to ordinary calorie restriction, with low-to-moderate certainty. TRE showed a small cholesterol rise compared with whole-day fasting. https://bmjgroup.com/intermittent-fasting-comparable-to-traditional-diets-for-weight-loss/
   - Liu, NEJM 2022 (n=139, 12 months): 8-hour TRE plus calorie restriction was no better than calorie restriction alone (−1.8 kg, CI −4.0 to 0.4). No safety signal is mentioned in the summaries I saw. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35443107/

**Bottom line from primary sources:** This is an observational association, a CVD-only signal with a wide CI, and the eating window was measured on 2 days rather than as a sustained deliberate 16:8 regimen. All-cause mortality was null. It is weak evidence that 16:8 is harmful for a healthy 45-year-old. RCTs show modest weight benefit, about equal to calorie restriction.

**Unsure of**
- I couldn't get the absolute number of CVD deaths in the <8 h group or the full covariate list. The paywalled paper and the poster weren't accessible.
- It's unclear whether the published version adjusted for diet quality or shift work.
- I didn't verify the BMJ correction (bmj.r1737).
- There are no long-term RCTs of TRE on hard cardiovascular outcomes.

**Researcher report: press, forums and community write-ups**

**Findings**

1. **Where the headline comes from.** The 91% figure is from an American Heart Association press release about a conference poster at EPI|Lifestyle in March 2024 (Chen, Zhong et al., Shanghai Jiao Tong). The work was not peer-reviewed at that point. It used NHANES 2003–2018 data on about 20,000 adults. People were placed in eating-window groups using **two 24-hour dietary recalls**, and deaths were tracked for a median of 8 years. The press release says the result does not show causation. https://newsroom.heart.org/news/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-linked-to-a-91-higher-risk-of-cardiovascular-death?print=1
2. **The numbers have shifted between versions.** HealthDay reported HR 1.96 from the abstract and 840 cardiovascular deaths in total. That works out to about 4% of the whole cohort over 8 years. https://www.healthday.com/healthpro-news/cardiovascular-diseases/time-restricted-eating-linked-to-cardiovascular-mortality The paper came out in August 2025 in *Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome* (Chen et al., 2025; PubMed ID 40849219) with HR 2.35 (95% CI 1.39–3.98) against a 12–14 h reference. It found **no link with deaths from all causes or from cancer**, and the authors themselves raise residual confounding. https://medicaldialogues.in/amp/diet-nutrition/news/intermittent-fasting-under-8-hours-may-raise-heart-death-risk-by-135-percent-study-finds-153915
3. **UK Science Media Centre experts were critical.** Spiegelhalter said the abstract "should not have been graced with a press release." McConway said two days of recall can't stand in for long-term eating habits. Frayn and Mellor raised reverse causation (people already at risk cutting their eating window) and missing body-weight data. Sanders suggested shift work as a confounder. https://www.sciencemediacentre.org/expert-reaction-to-conference-abstract-about-time-restricted-eating-and-cardiovascular-death/
4. **A rebuttal from 34 time-restricted eating researchers.** They point out that the under-8 h group had 60% more smokers and 3.5 times the share of Black participants (23.2% vs 6.6%). That group was only about 2% of the sample, and short windows may partly reflect incomplete food records. They also cite more than 100 trials with no serious harms. Caveat: the signatories, including Panda, Varady and Peterson, work in this field. https://blog.mycircadianclock.org/debunking-misleading-claims-the-truth-behind-the-headlines-on-time-restricted-eating-and-cardiovascular-risk/ and https://nutritioninsight.com/news/scientists-dispute-study-linking-time-restricted-eating-to-poor-heart-health.html
5. **Other commentators.** Krumholz (Yale) called the study "exploratory" (https://www.statnews.com/2024/03/19/intermittent-fasting-study-heart-risk/). Meyerowitz-Katz says the study doesn't really measure intermittent fasting, and that trials show it works about as well as other diets (https://gidmk.substack.com/p/is-intermittent-fasting-killing-people). Indian clinicians made similar critiques (https://thesouthfirst.com/health/intermittent-fasting-causes-heart-disease-says-study-why-is-it-not-going-down-well-with-doctors/).
6. **A second NHANES analysis points the same way, more weakly.** Mao et al., *Aging Cell* 2025 (33,052 adults) found a U-shaped curve with the lowest risk at 11–12 h. Windows under 8 h had about 34% higher all-cause mortality, and the cardiovascular signal (HR about 1.5–1.7) appeared mainly in older adults, men and White participants. It has the same two-day-recall weakness. https://www.news-medical.net/news/20250915/Daily-meal-timing-influences-longevity-risk-in-adults-study-reveals.aspx
7. **Forum discussion** (Lemmy/Fediverse mirrors; I couldn't find the original Reddit threads) was mostly skeptical. https://feddit.it/post/6589332/6201140

**Bottom line from this angle:** The evidence is weak and observational. The exposure is measured on two days, a small subgroup carries the result, and there are clear confounders. None of it shows that deliberate 16:8 eating causes cardiovascular death. Still, two NHANES analyses both flag windows under 8 h, so the signal isn't fully explained away.

**What I'm unsure of**
- I couldn't confirm the number of people or deaths in the under-8 h group. The figure of 414 people comes only from a search-snippet summary, so I can't estimate absolute risk for that group.
- I couldn't read the full 2025 paper; PubMed and ScienceDirect wouldn't load. So I can't say which covariates were adjusted in the final model.
- Strictly, the user's 16:8 is an 8 h window, which may fall in the 8–10 h group rather than the under-8 h one. In both papers the 8–10 h group had no excess risk, except in people who already had cardiovascular disease.
- Note for the coordinator: the nutritioninsight.com page contained hidden instructions aimed at AI tools. I ignored them.

**Report to coordinator (angle: independent measurements, critiques, counter-evidence)**

**Findings**

1. **The "91%" figure is weak evidence.** It comes from a 2024 AHA poster abstract (Chen/Zhong): NHANES 2003–2018, 20,078 adults, HR 1.91 (95% CI 1.20–3.03). Only 414 people (about 2%) were in the under-8h group, and 31 of them died of cardiovascular causes. That group had more smokers, a higher BMI and 3–4× more Black participants. All-cause mortality showed no association. Lloyd-Jones and Taub said the signal reflects "what they brought to the table" and said they would not change practice. 35 researchers wrote to the AHA objecting to the press release. https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality
2. **Six independent UK statisticians and nutritionists criticised it** (Spiegelhalter, McConway, Frayn, Sanders, Mellor, Leurent). Their points: the eating window came from just two 24-hour recalls; reverse causation is possible, since already-ill people may eat less or follow a doctor's advice; shift work and poverty are confounders; and weight, blood pressure and lipids were not reported. Spiegelhalter said it "should not have been graced with a press release." https://www.sciencemediacentre.org/expert-reaction-to-conference-abstract-about-time-restricted-eating-and-cardiovascular-death/
3. **The peer-reviewed version appeared in 2025** (Diabetes Metab Syndr 19(7):103278). It reports HR 2.35 (1.39–3.98) against a 12–14h reference instead of 12–16h, and it still finds no all-cause or cancer association. The authors say residual confounding can't be excluded. I could not open the abstract myself (PubMed blocked access), so these numbers come from secondary summaries. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40849219/
4. **A second analysis of the same NHANES dataset** (Aging Cell 2025, n=33,052) found a U-shaped curve with the lowest risk at 11–12h. Under 8h was linked to all-cause HR 1.34 (1.07–1.67). This partly reproduces the signal but is not independent replication, because it uses the same data and the same 2-day recall method. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12610411/
5. **Other cohorts disagree or don't test the question.** In a UK cohort (n=2,945, 22-year follow-up), eating-window length was not linked to mortality (HR 1.00). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12411609 In NutriNet-Santé (n=103k), a longer overnight fast was linked to lower cerebrovascular risk. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9593955/
6. **Trials show neutral to modestly beneficial effects on risk factors, with no hard-outcome data.** A BMJ 2025 network meta-analysis (99 RCTs) found small weight benefits and no clear cardiometabolic differences compared with calorie restriction. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12175170/ A 2024 meta-analysis found small LDL and blood pressure improvements. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39519533/
7. **Lean-mass loss is the plausible concern.** The TREAT RCT (16:8, n=116) found a significant loss of appendicular lean mass compared with controls, and no extra weight loss. https://www.hawaii.edu/news/2020/10/09/intermittent-fasting-study/

**What the claim is based on**
- **What it was:** A 2024 conference abstract, not peer-reviewed. It used US survey data (NHANES) on about 20,000 adults, and each person's eating window was judged from just **two days of recalled meals**. People who ate within less than 8 hours had a 91% higher risk of dying from heart disease than people eating over 12–16 hours. It found no rise in deaths overall. ([AHA](https://newsroom.heart.org/news/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-linked-to-a-91-higher-risk-of-cardiovascular-death?print=1))
- **How small:** Only 414 people, about 2% of the sample, ate within under 8 hours, and 31 of them died of heart disease. ([TCTMD](https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality))
- **Who was in that group:** It had about 60% more smokers, more people with higher weight, and far more Black participants than the comparison group. That suggests it caught people with irregular meals, such as shift workers, rather than people deliberately doing 16:8. 34 researchers signed an open letter objecting to the publicity. ([letter summary](https://blog.mycircadianclock.org/debunking-misleading-claims-the-truth-behind-the-headlines-on-time-restricted-eating-and-cardiovascular-risk/), [JAMA](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2817556))
- **The published version (2025):** It uses a different comparison group (12–14 hours) and reports a 2.35 hazard ratio. Even the authors say the link may come from other factors they couldn't fully account for, not from the short eating window. ([Medical Dialogues](https://medicaldialogues.in/diet-nutrition/news/intermittent-fasting-under-8-hours-may-raise-heart-death-risk-by-135-percent-study-finds-153915), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40849219/))
- **Another analysis of the same survey:** Under-8-hour windows were linked to more deaths mainly in people 65 and older. There was no significant link in adults under 65 once other factors were accounted for. ([Aging Cell](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12610411/))

**What the trials show**
- In a review of 99 trials, intermittent fasting worked about as well as ordinary calorie cutting for weight and heart-risk markers, with low-to-moderate certainty. ([BMJ](https://bmjgroup.com/intermittent-fasting-comparable-to-traditional-diets-for-weight-loss/))
- 16:8 eating doesn't seem to help much beyond eating less overall. It added nothing over calorie restriction alone in a 12-month trial ([NEJM](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35443107/)). It produced no metabolic benefit when calories stayed the same ([ChronoFast](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2025/12/251228020018.htm)).

- If you develop heart disease, talk to your doctor before continuing.

**Report: official and primary sources**

There are two separate slowdowns, and they multiply. First, an emulated x86 build of Node runs everything. Second, `node_modules`, which has a huge number of files, sits on a bind mount that has to cross from macOS into Docker's Linux VM. Linux laptops have neither problem.

**Findings**

1. **The image runs under emulation.** Docker says emulation "can be much slower than native builds," and worst for compute-heavy work. https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/
   - The official `node` image is published for arm64v8 as well as amd64. So `--platform linux/amd64` makes the whole Node runtime emulated, not just the one x86 dependency. https://hub.docker.com/_/node
2. **Rosetta needs a specific setup.** Rosetta (Apple's x86 translator) runs amd64 containers much faster than the older QEMU emulator, but it only works when Docker Desktop uses the Apple Virtualization framework.
   - The settings page says the Rosetta option is available only with that framework and lists its Mac default as "Disabled." https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/
   - The 4.25 announcement says Rosetta is "enabled by default on macOS 14.1 and newer" and gives "near-native" speed. That speed is Docker's own claim; the post shows no benchmark. https://www.docker.com/blog/docker-desktop-4-25/
   - The Docker VMM page says "Docker VMM does not currently support Rosetta, so emulation of amd64 architectures is slow." If Docker VMM is selected, amd64 work falls back to slow emulation. https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/vmm/
   - Docker's performance blog recommends the Apple Virtualization framework for running Intel images. https://www.docker.com/blog/what-are-the-latest-docker-desktop-enterprise-grade-performance-optimizations/
3. **Bind mounts are slow on Mac.** VS Code's docs say bind mounts on macOS are slower because containers run inside a VM, and that write-heavy folders like `node_modules` suffer most. They recommend putting `node_modules` in a named volume (example config included) or using "Clone Repository in Container Volume." https://code.visualstudio.com/remote/advancedcontainers/improve-performance
4. **VirtioFS is already the default file sharing on Mac.** Docker improved its caching and I/O in 4.31–4.33. https://www.docker.com/blog/what-are-the-latest-docker-desktop-enterprise-grade-performance-optimizations/
5. **Synchronized file shares are another option.** They keep a copy of the project on ext4 inside the VM, and the docs suggest excluding `node_modules` with `.syncignore`. Docker's launch post claims 2–10x faster file operations. It needs 4.27 or later and, according to the launch post, a Pro, Team or Business plan; the current docs page doesn't mention a plan requirement. https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/synchronized-file-sharing/ and https://www.docker.com/blog/announcing-synchronized-file-shares/
6. **Rosetta's future.** Apple says that from macOS 27, Intel translation for Linux VMs is built into macOS and no separate Rosetta install is needed. Apple hasn't said this feature continues past macOS 27; its general Rosetta support ends then. https://developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/documentation/virtualization/running-intel-binaries-in-linux-vms.md and https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/787530

**Recommended actions, best first**
- Build for arm64 natively, and isolate or replace the x86-only dependency (for example, run only that piece in a separate amd64 container).
- If you must stay on amd64: choose Apple Virtualization framework and turn Rosetta on.
- Put `node_modules` in a named volume, or the whole source tree, or use synchronized file shares.

**What I'm unsure of**
- Official docs disagree on whether Rosetta is on by default. Check the actual settings on the Mac.
- The VMM docs page cites Docker Desktop versions 4.86 and 4.98, which I couldn't verify against release notes.
- I found no official benchmark that splits the 5–10x slowdown between emulation and file I/O. Timing a run with `node_modules` in a volume, then a run on a native arm64 image, would show which matters more.
- The "2–10x" and "near-native" figures are Docker's own claims.
- I don't know which dependency needs x86, so I can't say if an arm64 build of it exists.

**Report: press, forums, issue trackers and community write-ups**

Two separate slowdowns are probably stacking up. Linux laptops have neither: there, bind mounts are native and amd64 code runs natively.

**1. `node_modules` on a macOS bind mount (file I/O cost)**
- On a Mac, Docker runs containers inside a Linux VM. Every file access on a bind mount crosses from macOS into the VM, and `node_modules` is the worst case because it is tens of thousands of small files. Volumes that live inside the VM are fast. https://orbstack.dev/blog/fast-filesystem

# Why your dev container is slow on the Mac, and how to fix it

Two separate costs multiply on your Mac. Your Linux colleagues have neither.

## 1. Node runs under x86 emulation

`--platform linux/amd64` emulates the entire Node runtime (npm, bundler, dev server), not just the one x86 dependency. The official `node` image also ships for arm64 (https://hub.docker.com/_/node). Docker says emulation "can be much slower" (https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/).

- **Rosetta** is the fast emulator, and it requires the Apple Virtualization framework (https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/).
- **QEMU** is the fallback, and users report it is roughly 10× slower again (https://zerokspot.com/weblog/2023/11/14/rosetta-docker-desktop-feels-broken/).
- **Docker VMM** has no Rosetta support (https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/vmm/).
- **Known problems:** Rosetta has pegged the CPU with Vite/Rollup and lacks AVX (https://github.com/docker/roadmap/issues/384), and npm installs have hung on amd64 `node:20` (https://github.com/nodejs/docker-node/issues/1946).

## 2. `node_modules` on a bind mount

Every file access crosses from macOS into Docker's Linux VM, and `node_modules` contains tens of thousands of small files. In one measurement on the same project, `npm install` took:

| Setup | Time |
|---|---|
| Native | 4.0 s |
| Bind mount | 21.9 s |
| Bind mount + named volume for `node_modules` | 7.0 s |

Source: https://github.com/sparkfabrik/sparkdock/issues/61. VS Code recommends the same named-volume fix (https://code.visualstudio.com/remote/advancedcontainers/improve-performance).

## What to do, in order

1. **Build for arm64.** Drop the platform flag and isolate the x86-only dependency, for example in a small amd64 sidecar container. This is easy if the dependency is a CLI tool and harder if it's a native Node addon. DDEV also recommends native arm64 (https://ddev.com/blog/amd64-on-apple-silicon-ddev/).
2. **Put `node_modules` in a named volume** and bind-mount only the source.
3. **If you must stay on amd64,** open Docker Desktop settings and confirm three things: Apple Virtualization framework is selected (not Docker VMM), "Use Rosetta" is on, and VirtioFS is on. Docker's docs disagree on whether Rosetta is on by default (https://www.docker.com/blog/docker-desktop-4-25/), so check rather than assume.
4. **Upgrade from Node 20.** It reached end of life on 2026-04-30.
5. **Optional:** OrbStack (https://orbstack.dev/blog/fast-filesystem) or Docker's paid Synchronized File Shares (https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/synchronized-file-sharing/). Benchmark these yourself, because the vendors' speed claims are unaudited.

## Long-term risk

Apple's general Rosetta support ends with macOS 27. Built-in Intel translation for Linux VMs isn't promised beyond that (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/787530). This makes staying on amd64 a dead end.

## Confirm which cause matters most

No source measures both causes together. Run `time npm install` for each of the four combinations of {bind mount, volume} × {amd64, arm64} to see how much each contributes on your machine.

**Short answer: no. WAL mode on a shared NFS mount does not work. Switching to rollback mode could make it run, but it still wouldn't be safe enough for production.**

**Why WAL breaks across hosts**
- SQLite's documentation says plainly: "All processes using a database must be on the same host… WAL does not work over a network filesystem." WAL coordinates through a memory-mapped `-shm` index, and separate machines cannot share memory. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- NFS doesn't keep memory-mapped files in sync between clients. Red Hat closed the related bug as WONTFIX, noting that NFS servers don't track which clients have a file mapped. https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=179911
- This has happened in practice. OpenAI's Codex documentation says Linux hosts sharing an NFS home can corrupt a WAL-mode SQLite database, so Codex switches to rollback mode on NFS. https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/environments/network-file-systems

**Why rollback mode is still risky**
- Rollback mode depends on file locks working correctly over NFS. SQLite's FAQ says to avoid putting the database on NFS when multiple processes may access it at the same time. https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html, https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html
- SQLite isn't tested over a network, and failures are rare and hard to reproduce, so passing your own tests proves little. https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
- During a network blip, NFSv4 locks can expire. Current kernels then return I/O errors to the application. Older kernels, or the `recover_lost_locks` setting, can let two servers write at the same time. https://access.redhat.com/solutions/1179643
- Performance: every transaction locks the whole database and takes several network round trips. SQLite says to use a client/server database when several servers write to the same data. https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html

**What I'd do instead**
1. **Use PostgreSQL.** It's the simplest choice for three servers and 20 writes per second, and it's SQLite's own first suggestion. https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
2. **Or keep SQLite on one host's local disk** with WAL mode, and have the other two servers send reads and writes through a small service on that host. https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
3. **Or use replicated SQLite:**
   - rqlite (https://rqlite.io/docs/faq/) or dqlite (https://github.com/canonical/dqlite) replicate with Raft.
   - LiteFS has one writer and replicates asynchronously, so a failover can lose the most recent writes. https://docs.fly.io/litefs/how-it-works

If you go ahead with NFS anyway, use rollback (DELETE) mode. First, test that a lock taken on one host actually blocks the other hosts, and run that test under failure conditions too. https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-09-08-detect-unsafe-nfs-smb-embedded-database-locking/markdown

**Other sources consulted:** https://www.sqlite.org/lockingv3.html, https://www.sqlite.org/atomiccommit.html, https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/nfs.5.html, https://nfs.sourceforge.net/, https://docs.gotosocial.org/en/latest/advanced/sqlite-networked-storage/, https://mail-archive.com/sqlite-users@mailinglists.sqlite.org/msg56864.html, https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=629296

# No. WAL mode on a shared NFS mount across three servers will not work reliably.

All three researchers came to the same conclusion, and it rests mainly on SQLite's own documentation.

## Why

**1. WAL cannot work across hosts.** WAL coordinates readers and writers through a shared-memory index (the `-shm` file, accessed via mmap). Processes on different machines cannot share memory. SQLite's docs say: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." The `-shm` file is never fsynced and uses the host's byte order, so it was never meant to be shared between machines.
- https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/walformat.html

**2. NFS itself is a corruption risk, even without WAL.** SQLite's docs say network use is untested and "at the user's risk." They also say locks "have been known to operate incorrectly… This has led to database corruption," and they name NFS specifically.
- https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html

On the NFS side, Linux guarantees cache consistency only at file open and close, and it gives no mmap coherence between clients.
- https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/nfs.5.html

NFSv4 locks are held on a lease, and the server can revoke them if a client loses contact.
- https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7530

**3. Passing tests prove little.** In one report, two Grafana servers shared SQLite on NFS without problems for two weeks, and then the database became corrupted. SQLite maintainers warn that NFS can claim a lock or a commit succeeded when it didn't, and the damage may only show up later.
- https://community.grafana.com/t/two-grafana-servers-with-single-sqlite3-databse-on-nfs/2734
- https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/02c1a784a2830a3d?raw

**Counter-evidence:** one forum user runs SQLite on NFSv4 with up to 12 hosts and reports "very few" problems. This is probably rollback mode, not WAL, and they say it limits scaling. Nobody has published measured failure rates.
- https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/341635c1ff

## What to do instead

At 20 writes per second, either of these is simple:

1. **Use Postgres or MySQL.** This is the standard fix, and SQLite's own docs recommend it for multi-server writes.
   - https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html
2. **Keep SQLite on one server's local disk**, with WAL enabled, and have the other two servers send reads and writes to it through an API. One host can easily handle 20 writes per second.

**Avoid this option:** rollback-journal mode on NFS. SQLite lists it as allowed (many readers or one writer, never both at once), but every write would need a lock round-trip over the network. You would also still depend on your NFS server's locking being correct, so you'd need cross-host fault testing and reliable backups. Never use the `nolock` or `local_lock` mount options for this, because each client then sees only its own locks.

**Decision:** No, don't do it. Running SQLite in WAL mode on a shared NFS mount, with three hosts writing, won't work reliably. Instead, either keep SQLite on one server's local disk and have the other two servers reach it through an API, or move to Postgres/MySQL.

The `-shm` file is never fsynced and is written in the host's own byte order (https://www.sqlite.org/walformat.html). Linux NFS developers likewise say mmap'd files are never guaranteed coherent between clients (https://patchwork.kernel.org/comment/12578611/, https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/nfs.5.html). This follows from how WAL is designed, so it holds on your mount as on any other. A test that appears to pass proves nothing; drh calls such tests insufficiently thorough (https://mail-archive.com/sqlite-users@mailinglists.sqlite.org/msg108685.html). # 28 April 2025 Iberian blackout: established causes and open disputes

**Caveat:** I couldn't extract text from the official report PDFs, so technical details below come from ENTSO‑E's web pages, official press notes, and trade-press summaries of the reports. Check the details against the [final report PDF](https://eepublicdownloads.blob.core.windows.net/public-cdn-container/clean-documents/Publications/2025/iberian-blackout/Final%20Report%20on%20the%20Grid%20Incident%20in%20Spain%20and%20Portugal%20on%2028%20April%202025.pdf) before the brief goes out.

## Established by official investigations

- **ENTSO‑E expert panel, final report (20 Mar 2026)** [1]: no single cause. The factors were oscillations, gaps in voltage and reactive-power control, differing voltage-regulation practices, rapid output cuts and generator disconnections in Spain, and uneven stabilisation capabilities. Together they caused fast voltage rises and a cascade of generator trips. It was the first blackout of this kind in Continental Europe.
- **Sequence, from the factual report (3 Oct 2025)** [2][3]:
  - A 0.63 Hz oscillation (12:03–12:08) and a 0.21 Hz inter-area oscillation (12:19–12:22) were damped, but the damping measures raised Iberian voltage.
  - Trips began at 12:32:57 and exceeded 2.5 GW by 12:33:18, with voltage above 435 kV.
  - Iberia lost synchronism with Europe at 12:33:19. Load shedding could not stop a collapse driven by overvoltage.
- **Deficiencies the final report found** [3][4][5]:
  - Several synchronous units hit their reactive-power reference less than 75% of the time.
  - Shunt reactors were switched by hand.
  - Under Spanish rules, renewables ran at a fixed power factor.
  - Spain's 400 kV band allowed up to 435 kV, leaving little margin before protection trips.
  - At least 10 disconnections didn't meet requirements.
  - The voltage-control rule (PO 7.4) set no dynamic-performance requirements for conventional generators.
- **Spanish government committee (Jun 2025)** [6]: the cause was multifactorial. Voltage-control resources were either not scheduled in sufficient amount, or did not deliver what was scheduled, or both. Some disconnections appeared improper.
- **Cyberattack ruled out:** the Audiencia Nacional (Spain's national court) provisionally closed its case in January 2026, relying on reports from INCIBE and CCN, Spain's national cybersecurity agencies [6].

## Contested or unresolved

- **Who is responsible:** ENTSO‑E says assigning blame is outside its remit [7].
  - REE (the Spanish TSO) says it committed no breach and that its scheduling is not among the causes [7].
  - Utilities (Aelec, Endesa) blame poor scheduling of synchronous generation by REE [8][9].
  - In April 2026, CNMC (the Spanish regulator) opened sanction proceedings, including a "very serious" case against REE. It stressed this does not attribute the cause to anyone [10]. I found no outcome as of November 2026 [11].
- **Unexplained:**
  - Why generators missed their reactive-power setpoints [7].
  - Why about 500 MW of output fell at the start, and what caused most of the overvoltage trips [5].
  - Data gaps include unmonitored PV below 1 MW [3].
- **Source of the oscillation:** REE named a PV plant in Badajoz [12]. ENTSO‑E points to converter-driven instability in southern Spain [3]. Iberdrola is suing REE over being blamed [13].

1. **The 91% figure comes from a conference poster, not a peer-reviewed paper.** It was Abstract P192 from Chen and Zhong at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, presented at AHA EPI|Lifestyle in March 2024. They used NHANES 2003–2018 with death records through 2019: about 20,078 adults, median follow-up 8 years, 840 cardiovascular deaths. Eating in under 8 hours vs 12–16 hours gave HR 1.91 (95% CI 1.20–3.03) for cardiovascular death. Eating window was not linked to all-cause death. The AHA's own release labels it preliminary and not peer-reviewed. It says the eating window came from just **two 24-hour dietary recalls**, diet quality wasn't assessed, and baseline characteristics weren't compared. The senior author said it "does not mean that time-restricted eating caused cardiovascular death." https://newsroom.heart.org/news/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-linked-to-a-91-higher-risk-of-cardiovascular-death?print=1
   - A HealthDay report gives slightly different HRs (1.96), which matches the AHA note that the poster's numbers were revised. https://www.healthday.com/healthpro-news/cardiovascular-diseases/time-restricted-eating-linked-to-cardiovascular-mortality
2. **The peer-reviewed version** is Chen … Manson, Zhong, *Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome* 19(7):103278, August 2025, with 19,831 adults. Under 8 hours vs 12–14 hours gave **HR 2.35 (1.39–3.98) for cardiovascular death**. There was no link with all-cause or cancer death. The authors themselves say it's unclear whether the risk comes from the short window "or residual confounding." https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40849219/ (abstract obtained via Europe PMC; the full text is paywalled)
3. **An independent NHANES analysis** (Mao et al., *Aging Cell* 2025) had 33,052 adults, of whom only 1,473 had windows ≤8 hours. It found a U-shape, with the lowest risk at about 11–12 hours. For ≤8 hours, all-cause HR was 1.34 (1.07–1.67). The excess was mainly in adults 65 and over, and it was **not significant in young and middle-aged adults**. It uses the same dataset and the same two-day recall method, so it isn't truly independent replication. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12610411/
4. **Expert critique from the UK Science Media Centre** (Spiegelhalter, McConway, Frayn, Sanders, Mellor, Leurent) centred on four points:
   - Two recall days don't capture habits over 8 years.
   - Reverse causation: sick or at-risk people may eat less or be told to restrict.
   - Shift work, poverty and stress may be confounders.
   - Weight, blood pressure and lipids weren't reported.
   https://www.sciencemediacentre.org/expert-reaction-to-conference-abstract-about-time-restricted-eating-and-cardiovascular-death/
5. **Randomized trials** show no clear advantage for weight loss and no signal of cardiometabolic harm:

   - Semnani-Azad, BMJ 2025 (99 RCTs): intermittent fasting works about as well as ordinary calorie restriction; the trials were short. https://www.sciencemediacentre.org/expert-reaction-to-study-comparing-evidence-on-intermittent-fasting-and-traditional-calorie-reduction-diets-for-weight-loss/

- I couldn't get the 2025 paper's full text: how many people were in the <8 h group, how many cardiovascular deaths they had, which covariates were adjusted for (smoking, shift work, income), or what the sensitivity analyses showed. **What I'm unsure of**
- I couldn't access the full 2025 paper, so I don't know the group size or death count in the under-8 h group, or the exact adjustments.
- I don't know whether the published version fixed the smoking adjustment.
- The critics' letter comes from researchers invested in TRE.
- I found no Reddit threads.
- A strict 16:8 is right at the 8 h boundary. It's unclear whether that falls in the "<8 h" or "8–10 h" category.

- **Eating window measurement.** It came from just two 24-hour food recalls. Nobody was asked whether they fasted deliberately or did so for years. ## Short answer: this study alone isn't a reason to stop

**What the study actually found**
- The "91%" came from a March 2024 American Heart Association conference abstract. Researchers looked at about 20,000 people in a US national survey (NHANES). The 8-hour figure applied to people who ate within **less than** 8 hours a day, so your exact 16:8 wasn't the group tested. ([AHA](https://newsroom.heart.org/news/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-linked-to-a-91-higher-risk-of-cardiovascular-death?print=1))
- That group was only 414 people, and 31 of them died of heart disease. It had more smokers, a higher BMI, and three to four times more Black participants than the rest. ([TCTMD](https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality), [letter from 34 researchers](https://blog.mycircadianclock.org/debunking-misleading-claims-the-truth-behind-the-headlines-on-time-restricted-eating-and-cardiovascular-risk/))
- Eating windows came from just **two days** of self-reported food intake, then were assumed to hold for 8 or more years. The surveys ran from 2003 to 2018, so many of these people were probably shift workers or poor rather than deliberate fasters. Some short windows may simply be meals people forgot to report. ([Science Media Centre](https://www.sciencemediacentre.org/expert-reaction-to-conference-abstract-about-time-restricted-eating-and-cardiovascular-death/))
- The peer-reviewed 2025 version reported a hazard ratio of 2.35 (roughly 2.35 times the risk), but with a wide uncertainty range (1.39–3.98). It found no link with death from all causes, and the authors themselves say leftover confounding may explain it. ([Abstract](https://www.lifescience.net/publications/1424832/association-of-eating-duration-less-than-8-h-with-/))
- A separate NHANES analysis also found higher risk below 8 hours, but it has the same two-day weakness. ([Aging Cell](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12610411/))

**What the trials show**
- Randomized trials, mostly lasting 3 to 12 months, show small improvements in weight and blood pressure. No trial has measured heart attacks or deaths. ([BMJ](https://bmjgroup.com/intermittent-fasting-comparable-to-traditional-diets-for-weight-loss/), [Frontiers](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1631477/full))
- A one-year trial found 8-hour eating no better than plain calorie cutting. ([NEJM summary](https://pace-cme.org/2022/05/09/time-restricted-diet-is-not-more-beneficial-than-calorie-restriction-alone))
- Two real downsides showed up: some **loss of muscle** ([NEJM Journal Watch](https://clinician.nejm.org/fasting-shows-no-weight-loss-benefit-standard-meals-randomized-trial-nejm-jw.FW117079), [BMJ Medicine summary](https://www.news-medical.net/news/20260122/When-you-eat-matters-early-time-restricted-eating-improves-metabolic-health.aspx)), and higher LDL cholesterol with windows **shorter than** 8 hours.

**Rough sense of scale.** My own estimate: a healthy 45-year-old's chance of dying from heart disease over 8 years is around 1% or less. Even if the doubling were real, the added risk is under about 1 percentage point. ([CDC](https://cdc.gov/nchs/blog/posts/2021/11/19.html))

**Bottom line.** The evidence is weak (low quality, one small group, likely confounded). Experts disagree on what to do: some say keep going if it's working ([NBC](https://www.nbcnews.com/health/heart-health/intermittent-fasting-risk-cardiovascular-death-rcna143853)), others suggest a pause. If you continue, these steps address the real downsides:
- Don't shrink the window below 8 hours.
- Eat enough protein and do strength training to protect muscle.
- Focus on what you eat, not only when.
- Check your LDL and blood pressure at your next physical.
- An earlier window (for example 9:00–17:00) may be slightly better than a late one.

A 10–12 hour window is a reasonable fallback if you'd rather hedge. No guideline currently tells healthy people to stop.

- https://ddev.com/blog/amd64-with-rosetta-on-macos/

**Decision:** There are two stacked costs: bind-mount file I/O and x86 emulation. Fix them in this order:

1. **Move `node_modules` off the bind mount, now.** Mount it as a named volume (`- node_modules:/app/node_modules`) and run `npm install` inside the container. Do the same for cache and build folders. The trade-off is that the host no longer sees `node_modules`. This is cheap and easy to undo.
2. **Check Docker Desktop → Settings.** The VM manager should be **Apple Virtualization framework** (not Docker VMM), **Rosetta** should be on, and file sharing should be **VirtioFS**. Docker VMM does not support Rosetta, and without Rosetta amd64 falls back to QEMU, which is much slower.
3. **Hold on moving the image to arm64** until you've timed it. The likely best end state is an arm64 dev container, with the one x86-only dependency in its own amd64 service or stage.

**Rests on:**
- Mainardi (Jan 2025, M4 Pro, Docker Desktop 4.37, VZ + VirtioFS, npm install, mean of 3 runs) timed npm install three ways:
  - full bind mount: 9.53 s
  - `node_modules` in a named volume: 3.61 s
  - native: 3.37 s

  https://www.paolomainardi.com/posts/docker-performance-macos-2025/

- Docker's docs say the same: https://www.docker.com/blog/file-sharing-with-docker-desktop/
- GOV.UK saw builds go from about 19 s to about 4 s with this change: https://docs.publishing.service.gov.uk/repos/govuk-docker/adr/0003-use-docker-volumes-for-improved-macos-performance.html
- Emulation costs: https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/vmm/, https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/, https://www.docker.com/blog/docker-desktop-4-26/
- Arm64 for everything except the x86 service: https://ddev.com/blog/amd64-with-rosetta-on-macos/

**Not verified:**
- Whether your Docker Desktop is using Rosetta or QEMU. Docker's sources disagree on the default (https://www.docker.com/blog/docker-desktop-4-25/ vs https://docs.docker.com/settings-and-maintenance/settings/).
- A press report says Docker VMM became the default in October 2026, which would turn Rosetta off. It is unconfirmed: https://www.techtimes.com/articles/324240/20260813/docker-replaces-its-virtualization-engine-vmm-beta-live-mac-windows.htm
- How much of your 5–10x comes from emulation. Nobody has measured amd64 Node under Rosetta vs QEMU vs arm64 in a controlled way.
- Whether the x86 dependency needs AVX. Rosetta doesn't support it: https://github.com/docker/roadmap/issues/384
- Rosetta has known npm and Vite hangs and CPU pinning: https://github.com/nodejs/docker-node/issues/1946

**Next check:** Open Settings and read the VM manager and Rosetta values. That takes seconds. Then, with `node_modules` in a volume, time `npm install` and dev-server startup on amd64 vs arm64. If arm64 is much faster, split out the x86 dependency.

**No, this isn't safe.** Your plan uses WAL, which simply doesn't work across hosts. Even without WAL, SQLite's developers advise against having several machines share a database over NFS.

**Why WAL fails here**
- WAL coordinates connections through shared memory (the `-shm` file, which SQLite memory-maps). SQLite's docs say "all processes using a database must be on the same host… WAL does not work over a network filesystem." https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- Richard Hipp, SQLite's author, says WAL will "malfunction" when clients are on different hosts. If a test seemed to work, the test wasn't thorough enough. https://mail-archive.com/sqlite-users@mailinglists.sqlite.org/msg108685.html
- NFS doesn't keep memory-mapped files in sync between clients. https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=179911
- OpenAI's Codex docs say multiple hosts opening the same WAL database over NFS can corrupt it. Codex switches to DELETE (rollback) mode to avoid this. https://learn.chatgpt.com/codex/environments/network-file-systems

**Rollback mode is still risky**
- SQLite says locking on network filesystems is often buggy, and that a lock failure can let two hosts write at once and corrupt the file. https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html, https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html, https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html, https://www.sqlite.org/lockingv3.html, https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
- On NFSv4, a client can lose its locks if its lease expires, for example during a network blip. Writes then fail with EIO, and turning lock recovery back on "may cause data corruption." https://access.redhat.com/solutions/1179643
- The corruption can stay hidden and show up later. https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/02c1a784a2830a3d?raw
- Grafana users who shared a SQLite file over NFS reported corruption after two weeks. https://community.grafana.com/t/two-grafana-servers-with-single-sqlite3-databse-on-nfs/2734
- GoToSocial doesn't support SQLite on NFS at all. https://docs.gotosocial.org/en/latest/advanced/sqlite-networked-storage/
- One long-running user did fine over NFS, but only because their server honored locks and syncs exactly, and they still had some problems. https://mail-archive.com/sqlite-users@mailinglists.sqlite.org/msg111568.html

**What to do instead** (20 writes/sec is easy for any of these)
1. **PostgreSQL.** This is the best fit for three app servers writing to one database. https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html
2. **One server owns the SQLite file** on its local disk, in WAL mode, and the other two send reads and writes to it through an internal API. This is SQLite's own recommended "proxy" setup. https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
3. **Replicated SQLite**, where all writes go through one leader node:
   - rqlite: https://rqlite.io/docs/faq/
   - dqlite: https://canonical.com/dqlite/docs/explanation/replication
   - LiteFS: https://docs.fly.io/litefs/how-it-works

If you keep any SQLite on NFS, first test whether a lock taken on one host really blocks the others, across server restarts and network drops. https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-09-08-detect-unsafe-nfs-smb-embedded-database-locking/view

4. **The FAQ says** to avoid NFS "if multiple processes might try to access the file at the same time," because fcntl() locking is broken on many NFS implementations. https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html
5. **The page on use over a network** calls this "at your (and your customers') peril" and says SQLite is "not tested in across-a-network scenarios." It recommends one of three setups: (a) PostgreSQL or another client/server database; (b) keep the database in WAL mode on one host, with the other servers reaching it through a proxy on that host; (c) rollback-journal mode, as damage limitation only. https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
6. **When-to-use page:** avoid SQLite where one database is "accessed directly… and simultaneously from many computers over a network." https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html
7. **The locking page also warns** that fsync may not work properly on network filesystems. "Your best defense is to not use SQLite for files on a network filesystem." https://www.sqlite.org/lockingv3.html

**Takeaway for the coordinator:** WAL across three hosts is a hard no. Rollback mode over NFS is unsupported and risky, and failures show up silently and late. The community consensus is Postgres or MySQL, or SQLite on a single host behind a service.

# Report: SQLite on a shared NFS mount, three hosts writing in WAL mode (critiques and counter-evidence)

**Bottom line: it isn't safe as planned.** WAL mode across hosts is ruled out by how WAL is built. Rollback mode might work on a particular NFS setup, but it's unsupported and only acceptable after careful testing.

## Findings

1. **WAL can't work across machines.** SQLite's WAL docs say: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." WAL coordinates through a memory-mapped `-shm` file that is never fsynced, and separate hosts can't share that memory. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
2. **SQLite's own advice for network setups:** use a client/server database, or keep WAL access on one host behind a proxy, or use rollback mode. Quote: "Rely upon it at your (and your customers') peril." It also says network fsync "can be less robust than local filesystem sync" and that SQLite is not tested in this scenario. https://sqlite.org/useovernet.html
3. **Broken locking leads to corruption.** SQLite names NFS specifically as a filesystem with lock bugs that can corrupt data. https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html. The FAQ says "fcntl() file locking is broken on many NFS implementations." https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html
4. **NFS caching works against shared databases.** Close-to-open consistency gives no freshness guarantee while a file stays open. `noac` does not turn off data caching, and "there are still races." NLM locks are advisory only. With `nolock` or `local_lock`, locks only exclude processes on the same client. https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/nfs.5.html
5. **Field report, three-node cluster:** with GlusterFS, `integrity_check` "generally will show a bunch of problems after a short test." Fixing it took turning off write-behind and client caching. https://lists.gluster.org/pipermail/gluster-users/2018-March/033659.html
6. **WAL over NFS failing in practice:** Firefox profiles in WAL mode on NFS got "disk I/O error" when mapping `-shm`. The fix was an exclusive single-process VFS. https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=629296
7. **Counter-evidence:** a multi-node Raspberry Pi test against NFS, in rollback mode with `BEGIN EXCLUSIVE`, ended with correct counters. Experienced forum members said the test didn't prove much: it didn't exercise normal locking, and SQLite 3.17–3.32.2 had a COMMIT-retry bug. https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/4400357802?t=c
8. **Practitioner checklist:** use rollback mode only, "never use WAL across hosts." Run cross-host lock and fault-injection tests, and repeat them after any kernel or mount change. The article reports no measured results. https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-09-08-detect-unsafe-nfs-smb-embedded-database-locking/markdown
9. **Community consensus (anecdotal):** Plex and Unraid users keep reporting corrupted SQLite databases on network shares, and the standard advice is to keep databases on local disk.
10. **Performance (secondary):** search snippets of the FaaSFS paper (arXiv 2009.09845) say a TPC-C workload on NFS slowed about 10× going from one client to two, because whole-file cache invalidation causes false sharing. I couldn't read the PDF to confirm this, and it isn't SQLite-specific.

## What I'm unsure of

- I found no controlled study measuring corruption rates for NFSv4 plus a modern Linux client plus SQLite in rollback mode. All the evidence is official warnings and anecdotes.
- Whether 20 writes/s across 3 hosts in rollback mode would hold up on their specific NFS server and mount options. Throughput is also untested: every write takes an exclusive whole-database lock and goes through NFS fsync and cache revalidation.
- SQLite 3.51.0 added defences for locks broken by `close()`. That's a separate issue and doesn't address NFS.

**Recommendation from my angle:** don't share the file. Use Postgres or MySQL, or run SQLite on one host behind an API.

**Suggested wording:** "≈19% of crates directly use `unsafe` (May 2024). About a third call directly into such crates, and earlier research puts the share affected through dependencies above half."

**Decision:** No. Don't let three servers open one SQLite file over NFS. Use PostgreSQL or MySQL. If you want to keep SQLite, run it on local disk on one host and have the other two servers reach it through a small service or API.

This follows from how SQLite works, so it applies to your setup without needing a test.

- SQLite calls network use "at your (and your customers') peril," says it is untested there, and names NFS as the classic case of broken locking (https://sqlite.org/useovernet.html, https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html, https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html).

- When locking fails, the corruption is silent and shows up late.
- Each write would also take a whole-database lock with network round-trips, which is a poor fit for 20 writes per second (https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/c04bf5be0e).

**Not verified:** Nobody has measured how reliable rollback mode is on a modern Linux NFSv4 setup like yours. That would only matter if you insisted on sharing the file, and it still wouldn't make that a supported setup.

**Next check:** None needed. If you go the single-host route, put the SQLite file on that host's local disk, not on the NFS mount.

**Decision: No, the plan is not safe. Do not put the SQLite database on the shared NFS mount. Use PostgreSQL or MySQL, or keep SQLite on one server and have the other two reach it through an API or proxy on that host.**

Firefox hit this exact failure on NFS (https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=629296).

- SQLite names NFS specifically as a filesystem whose broken locking corrupts databases (https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html, https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html).
- It calls network use "at your (and your customers') peril" and says it is untested there (https://sqlite.org/useovernet.html).
- The Linux NFS client does not keep caches coherent between clients without application-level serialization (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/nfs.5.html).
- NFSv4 locks can be revoked when a lease lapses, so after a network stall two writers can each believe they hold the lock (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7530.html).
